medical.title: AI tools can simplify medical reports but still need human oversight
medical.summary: A team of researchers from the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) has evaluated various artificial intelligence (AI) language models to simplify medical reports and adapt them into clearer language for nonexpert audiences. This work will help patients better understand their health conditions and properly adhere to prescribed treatments.

medical.title: Brain stimulation reveals how language networks adapt in real time to disruption
medical.summary: When an important area of the human brain involved in language processing is temporarily disrupted, other areas of the brain take over much of its work. Researchers at Leipzig University and the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences (MPI CBS) in Leipzig have shown how flexibly the brain can maintain performance even in the face of acute disruption, and how different brain networks work together in real time to achieve this. The researchers have just published their new study in Nature Communications.

medical.title: Experimental cell therapy improves skin resilience, advancing treatments for skin injuries
medical.summary: In a phase 1 clinical trial, Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers say they have partially transformed ordinary human skin cells into volar skin—the durable skin found exclusively on the palms and soles that resists friction and pressure.

medical.title: Three-week Arctic operation shows blood products can survive harsh transport conditions and remain transfusion-ready
medical.summary: Getting blood products for transfusions to a battlefield in Canada's High Arctic is feasible but complex, according to newly published research in the journal Transfusion.

medical.title: A personality trait may provide clues to functioning in frontotemporal dementia
medical.summary: Frontotemporal dementia often results in early changes in personality or behavior before changes in cognitive skills. People with this condition who have lower levels of conscientiousness, a personality trait related to organization, reliability and planning, may be more likely to have problems with their ability to complete everyday activities, according to a study published in Neurology.

medical.title: How babies are born knowing the difference between day and night
medical.summary: Before a baby sees its first sunrise, it is already receiving signals about day and night. Melatonin, a hormone released mainly at night, can pass from the mother through the placenta. The placenta supplies the developing fetus with oxygen and nutrients.

medical.title: New MRI scan 'color codes' treatment-resistant cancer cells, sparing some patients from aggressive treatment
medical.summary: Scientists are developing a new MRI-based test that could spare thousands of cancer patients from aggressive radiotherapy treatment.

medical.title: Tiny sensor could track blood pressure continuously without inflatable cuff
medical.summary: A tiny sensor could one day measure blood pressure continuously, comfortably and accurately without an inflatable cuff. The device was developed by professors Amir Rosenthal and Daniel Lange of the Technion's Andrew and Erna Viterbi Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering, together with doctoral student Gil Gelbert. They published their findings in Nature Communications.

medical.title: Predicting long-term pain after freezing nerves in surgery
medical.summary: After thoracic surgery—any medical operation done inside the chest—patients can experience pain, soreness or numbness even years later. This is because the incisions cut through muscles and nerves on sensitive ribs, which can cause damage and inflammation.

medical.title: Daily, oral GLP-1 medication reduced episodes of sleep apnea in adults with excess weight
medical.summary: Adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and excess weight had significantly fewer episodes of breathing interruptions while sleeping after taking the daily oral GLP-1 medication orforglipron for one year, compared with adults in the placebo group, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

medical.title: What university campus sewage can reveal about the effects of exam stress
medical.summary: It is not often that scientists take a keen interest in the sewage produced by students. But a study of wastewater from a university campus in Australia is revealing insights into how exam stress affects the body that traditional surveys may miss.

medical.title: EEG analysis estimates depressive symptom severity in adults not receiving psychiatric treatment
medical.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba have developed a method that uses brainwave patterns to estimate the severity of self-reported depressive symptoms in adults who are not receiving treatment. The method examines how abrupt timing shifts in brain rhythms at one recording site are associated with those at another, and could support future screening and symptom monitoring. The work is published in Nature Mental Health.

medical.title: Norovirus No. 1 cause of cruise ship outbreaks for past 30 years, but other pathogens gaining
medical.summary: The gastrointestinal (GI) pathogen norovirus was the leading cause of infectious-disease outbreaks on cruise ships over the past 57 years, but respiratory pathogens such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 also emerged as important contributors, reveals a meta-analysis published in eClinicalMedicine.

medical.title: Resistance training key to maintaining muscle function during GLP-1 weight loss, study shows
medical.summary: A study has revealed that resistance (weight) training not only preserves lean and muscle mass but also increases strength in people taking weight-loss medication. Published in Nature Medicine, the Tirzepatide and Resistance Exercise (T-REx) study is the first to show the effects of combining a GLP-1 medicine and resistance training on body composition, muscle mass, strength and a range of cardiovascular health measures.

medical.title: Uncovering the regulators of inflammatory responses in macrophages
medical.summary: Macrophages are white blood cells that serve as the first line of defense against infections. When they encounter harmful pathogens or bacteria, macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming: significant metabolic changes that facilitate the production of inflammatory molecules.

medical.title: Almost one in four Americans believe misinformation about the cause of autism
medical.summary: Nearly a quarter of Americans believe that childhood vaccines and taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) during pregnancy cause autism, despite no evidence to support those claims, a survey published in JAMA Health Forum notes. The findings suggest that misinformation about autism persists and that better public health messaging is needed to combat it.

medical.title: Older female influencers challenging stereotypes around aging
medical.summary: Older female influencers are using social media to challenge long-held assumptions about women and aging, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

medical.title: New stem cell models reveal how earliest human placenta structures take shape
medical.summary: The placenta is essential for a healthy pregnancy, but the earliest steps of its formation have been hidden from scientific view. Now Columbia researchers led by Mijo Simunovic have created lab-grown organoids that reconstruct the earliest steps in human placenta formation, offering a powerful new tool for studying how pregnancy begins and why it often fails. The development of the 3D models is described in the current issue of Nature Cell Biology.

medical.title: Opioid use can become long-term following surgery
medical.summary: Opioids are effective medicines for severe pain following surgery, but prolonged use is associated with risks such as dependence and overdose. In his thesis, Claes Gedda at the Department of Clinical Sciences, Danderyd Hospital, Karolinska Institutet, investigated how common it is for patients in Sweden to continue using opioids after surgery, which patients are at higher risk, and whether usage following major surgery can be reduced.

medical.title: Blood pressure meds may improve therapy for ulcerative colitis
medical.summary: A class of blood pressure medications may improve a widely used treatment for ulcerative colitis, the most common type of inflammatory bowel disease, suggests a new study, led by Northwestern Medicine and Kiel University in Germany, of thousands of patients with the disease.

medical.title: HIV activism offers a roadmap for tackling weight stigma
medical.summary: Although HIV and obesity are not mirror images, lessons from the HIV response could accelerate fairer and more effective care for people living with obesity.

medical.title: Axonal defects linked to rare form of Parkinson's disease
medical.summary: A genetic mutation linked to Parkinson's disease produced abnormalities in a subset of nerve cells, offering a clue about the disease's causes, according to a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings offer new clues about how the neurodegenerative disorder begins and progresses, said D. James Surmeier, Ph.D., the Nathan Smith Davis professor and chair of neuroscience, who was a co-author of the study.

medical.title: Visual tests could indicate cognitive decline—study
medical.summary: Simple visual tests could be an early indicator of cognitive decline, a precursor to dementia, according to a new study published in the journal Brain Sciences.

medical.title: The butterfly effect: a brighter way to make paint?
medical.summary: Researchers are looking to butterflies in the search for coatings without harmful, chemical-based pigments The post The butterfly effect: a brighter way to make paint? appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas
science.summary: An international team of researchers, led by Jonathan Freundlich (University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory), has revealed how a dense cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas. By mapping the molecular gas in a galaxy group located 7 billion light-years away, they found that the galaxies in this group harbor, on average, gas reservoirs reduced by more than half compared to similar isolated galaxies. The results of this study are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

science.title: Antarctic water analysis reveals unexpected stability in dissolved organic carbon
science.summary: Researchers have analyzed water samples collected during two expeditions aboard the research icebreaker Polarstern to investigate how life and changing conditions on the Antarctic continental shelf affect carbon carried into the deep ocean. Published in Nature Communications, the study reveals a surprising finding: Despite intense biological activity and major changes in the water masses, the amount and make-up of dissolved organic matter remain almost unchanged.

science.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
science.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

science.title: Scientists discover new way to control magnetic waves for future quantum technologies
science.summary: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Ames National Laboratory have discovered a way to control the handedness of magnons, tiny magnetic waves that can carry information through materials. By changing the material's magnetic state with an external magnetic field, they were able to switch magnon behavior, a finding with potential applications in quantum information and quantum computing technologies. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters.

science.title: Classical–quantum light interactions could make complex quantum behavior easier to simulate
science.summary: An international collaboration demonstrates that classical nonlinear dynamics can drive single- and two-photon states to thermalize, opening new avenues for simulating complex quantum many-body systems within accessible optical architectures.

science.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
science.summary: Artificial intelligence use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy.

science.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
science.summary: A new study suggests that most of Earth's carbon originated in the outer solar system and didn't arrive here until the late stages of planetary development. The study, led by researchers at Yale and Columbia, is based upon an analysis of magma droplets called "melt inclusions" from historic volcano eruptions in Hawaii, including the Keanakākoʻi eruptions from 1500 to 1840 and the Kīlauea Iki eruption in 1959.

science.title: Poles of bacteria imaged in fine detail for the first time
science.summary: The poles, or ends, of rod-shaped bacteria have been imaged at molecular resolution for the first time in a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, used a new technique to keep live bacteria in place so the cells could be imaged without wriggling away.

science.title: New approach boosts plastic-eating enzyme's activity nearly tenfold
science.summary: Researchers from King's College London and Rutgers University in New Jersey created a modified enzyme (a protein that speeds up chemical reactions) that breaks down polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic 10 times quicker, using 10 times less enzyme. They accomplished this just by changing the liquid it works in and making small changes to the enzyme's structure.

science.title: Financial institutions tout sustainability while still funding high-carbon projects, review finds
science.summary: A review published in the International Journal of Managerial and Financial Accounting on the subject of greenwashing in financial services has found that financial institutions often claim environmental responsibility while continuing to finance high-carbon projects.

science.title: Protein-building RNA molecules reveal possible remnants of an ancestral genetic code
science.summary: The genetic code determines the correspondence between genetic instructions and amino acids—the building blocks that form proteins. How this correspondence arose is one of the major open questions in evolutionary biology. A study led by Dr. Lluís Ribas de Pouplana, ICREA researcher at IRB Barcelona, and Dr. Paul Schimmel, with the participation of researchers from MIT and Scripps Research, has identified conserved signals in transfer RNAs that could help reconstruct the early stages of this system.

science.title: Webb's controversial 'little red dots' may finally have an explanation
science.summary: Astronomers may have solved one of the biggest mysteries uncovered by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), using sophisticated simulations to show that enigmatic objects known as "little red dots" (LRDs) are likely the birthplaces of the first supermassive black holes.

science.title: Protein tails help shape mosquito cell-to-cell channels
science.summary: Cells share small molecules with their neighbors through tiny tunnels made of proteins arranged in a ring. Research at Nagoya University suggests that the tails of the proteins must link up to form an inner ring for the tunnel to become evenly round—a previously unknown step in how these cell-to-cell connections are built.

science.title: Two new howler monkey species discovered in the Amazon after 85 years
science.summary: Genetic research has uncovered two previously unknown species of howler monkey living in the Amazon rainforest, confirming the world's largest tropical forest is more biodiverse than scientists thought.

science.title: When the definition of sexual consent gets stretched
science.summary: Men in treatment for domestic violence have an elastic view of what constitutes consent in their partner, an UdeM study has found.

science.title: Repeatable laser measurements reveal 'forbidden' vibrations in single molecules without destroying them
science.summary: The possibility of controlling "forbidden" excitations of vibrations in molecules could form the basis of extremely accurate clocks, quantum bits and precise tests of the fundamental laws of physics. Researchers at the University of Basel have now identified and controlled such "forbidden" transitions in single isolated nitrogen molecules without destroying them.

science.title: Airborne imaging explores a mosaic of thawing permafrost
science.summary: Permafrost in many of Earth's northern regions is thawing, a process that unlocks greenhouse gases, threatens infrastructure, and could alter landscapes and ecosystems. The Arctic and subarctic are vast, and gaining a comprehensive picture of permafrost distribution is difficult, as it requires seeing under the ground. Now, with a new method that can map permafrost from the air, researchers may get a much more spatially cohesive view of permafrost thickness and distribution.

science.title: Reef biodiversity accounting to help scale up restoration
science.summary: To encourage new investments in more effective reef restoration activities, Australian scientists are recommending a new way of measuring biodiversity on coral reefs. A team of Australian environmental scientists led by James Cook University's distinguished professor Morgan Pratchett proposes the more rigorous and transparent framework in a paper published in the journal One Earth.

science.title: Leader still means man, and language does not change that, according to study
science.summary: Can gender-inclusive language weaken the deeply ingrained stereotype that a political leader is a man? A recent international study, conducted in 42 countries and involving researchers from SWPS University, shows that introducing such forms into language has little impact on how the public perceives political leaders.

science.title: NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities
science.summary: Launched nearly 50 years ago in 1977, NASA’s Voyager 1 on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will have traveled one light-day from Earth, which is more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, and any light from Earth would take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. NASA will highlight […]

science.title: Study finds links between bacteria in wastewater and chronic disease
science.summary: Bacteria found in wastewater may provide clues about community health, including rates of chronic disease, health behaviors and social conditions, according to a recent study from The Ohio State University.

science.title: Free-to-air TV failures add to data costs for remote Australian First Nations households
science.summary: Almost two in three respondents surveyed in Australia's remote First Nations communities did not have working free-to-air television, a study has found.

science.title: Q&A: 'AI has become a major force shaping our world,' says expert
science.summary: Artificial intelligence is reshaping research, economies, and everyday life at a remarkable speed. In this interview accompanying the new AI100 report, Iyad Rahwan reflects on the rise of generative AI, the growing concentration of AI power, and the challenges facing societies worldwide. He also explains why Europe must seize this "Sputnik moment" and why he remains optimistic about AI's potential to accelerate scientific discovery.

science.title: Archaeological trap: Fish can make skeletons appear hundreds of years too old
science.summary: The Danish town of Svendborg was once home to a Franciscan monastery. As at other monasteries in Denmark, it was considered highly prestigious to be buried as close to the monastery church as possible, preferably inside the church itself, for instance near the chapter house or along the cloister.

science.title: Ph.D. completion depends on reciprocal mix of candidate, supervision and institution, review finds
science.summary: Low Ph.D. completion rates remain a challenge in higher education, reflecting a complex interplay of individual, supervisory and institutional factors. Despite extensive research, few reviews have investigated the factors related to Ph.D. completion, with most focusing on isolated aspects, such as supervision or mental health.

environment.summary: Kenya’s fitness boom runs on activewear built for stretch, sweat and shine yet almost no one asks what’s actually in the fabric. By 7 a.m. on a Saturday, Riverside Square in Nairobi’s Westlands neighborhood is already filling up. Dozens arrive in matching leggings and sports bras, water bottles clipped to armbands, ready for a running […]

environment.summary: A recent Mongabay investigation by Elizabeth Claire Alberts and Andrés Alegría reveals that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a swath of deep sea regulated by the International Seabed Authority, has received a surge of claim applications filed with the United States for mineral exploration and exploitation. While the ISA, a U.N.-associated body, is […]

environment.title: ‘You need strong willpower’: IUCN’s Kazi Zenifar Azmiri on being a woman wildlife biologist
environment.summary: For more than a decade, Kazi Zenifar Azmiri has played a crucial part in protecting wildlife in Bangladesh. Zenifar is a program associate at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Her work centers primarily on the rescue and rehabilitation of threatened vultures like the white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Himalayan griffon vulture (Gyps […]

environment.title: Drought reshapes livelihoods of Kenya’s Daasanach pastoralists, study finds
environment.summary: The Daasanach people in the Turkana Basin of northern Kenya experienced the worst drought in 40 years between November 2020 and March 2023. The Daasanach are pastoralists who have lived semi-nomadically for roughly 6,000 years, supported by herds of livestock including cows, camels, donkeys, and goats. A group of researchers worked with the Daasanach to […]

environment.title: Greta Thunberg arrives at UN climate talks saying ‘everything we love is at stake’
environment.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Prominent climate change activist Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the U.N. climate meeting, where she emphasized the need to protect people and the planet over profits and power. This year’s meeting — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes after a year of climate-induced heat waves and other […]

environment.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
environment.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

environment.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
environment.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

environment.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
environment.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas
mix_items.summary: An international team of researchers, led by Jonathan Freundlich (University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory), has revealed how a dense cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas. By mapping the molecular gas in a galaxy group located 7 billion light-years away, they found that the galaxies in this group harbor, on average, gas reservoirs reduced by more than half compared to similar isolated galaxies. The results of this study are published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

mix_items.title: Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco
mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: AI tools can simplify medical reports but still need human oversight
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers from the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M) has evaluated various artificial intelligence (AI) language models to simplify medical reports and adapt them into clearer language for nonexpert audiences. This work will help patients better understand their health conditions and properly adhere to prescribed treatments.

mix_items.title: Antarctic water analysis reveals unexpected stability in dissolved organic carbon
mix_items.summary: Researchers have analyzed water samples collected during two expeditions aboard the research icebreaker Polarstern to investigate how life and changing conditions on the Antarctic continental shelf affect carbon carried into the deep ocean. Published in Nature Communications, the study reveals a surprising finding: Despite intense biological activity and major changes in the water masses, the amount and make-up of dissolved organic matter remain almost unchanged.

mix_items.title: When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores?
mix_items.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

mix_items.title: Brain stimulation reveals how language networks adapt in real time to disruption
mix_items.summary: When an important area of the human brain involved in language processing is temporarily disrupted, other areas of the brain take over much of its work. Researchers at Leipzig University and the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences (MPI CBS) in Leipzig have shown how flexibly the brain can maintain performance even in the face of acute disruption, and how different brain networks work together in real time to achieve this. The researchers have just published their new study in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover new way to control magnetic waves for future quantum technologies
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Ames National Laboratory have discovered a way to control the handedness of magnons, tiny magnetic waves that can carry information through materials. By changing the material's magnetic state with an external magnetic field, they were able to switch magnon behavior, a finding with potential applications in quantum information and quantum computing technologies. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters.

mix_items.title: Experimental cell therapy improves skin resilience, advancing treatments for skin injuries
mix_items.summary: In a phase 1 clinical trial, Johns Hopkins Medicine researchers say they have partially transformed ordinary human skin cells into volar skin—the durable skin found exclusively on the palms and soles that resists friction and pressure.

mix_items.title: Classical–quantum light interactions could make complex quantum behavior easier to simulate
mix_items.summary: An international collaboration demonstrates that classical nonlinear dynamics can drive single- and two-photon states to thermalize, opening new avenues for simulating complex quantum many-body systems within accessible optical architectures.

mix_items.title: Three-week Arctic operation shows blood products can survive harsh transport conditions and remain transfusion-ready
mix_items.summary: Getting blood products for transfusions to a battlefield in Canada's High Arctic is feasible but complex, according to newly published research in the journal Transfusion.

mix_items.title: AI use is now universal in higher education. Why are universities failing to adapt?
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence use among university students is now near-universal in many countries. Yet, as of a year ago, fewer than one in five universities in a 90-country UNESCO survey had a formal AI policy.

mix_items.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
mix_items.summary: A new study suggests that most of Earth's carbon originated in the outer solar system and didn't arrive here until the late stages of planetary development. The study, led by researchers at Yale and Columbia, is based upon an analysis of magma droplets called "melt inclusions" from historic volcano eruptions in Hawaii, including the Keanakākoʻi eruptions from 1500 to 1840 and the Kīlauea Iki eruption in 1959.

mix_items.title: Poles of bacteria imaged in fine detail for the first time
mix_items.summary: The poles, or ends, of rod-shaped bacteria have been imaged at molecular resolution for the first time in a new study led by UCL (University College London) researchers. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, used a new technique to keep live bacteria in place so the cells could be imaged without wriggling away.

mix_items.title: New approach boosts plastic-eating enzyme's activity nearly tenfold
mix_items.summary: Researchers from King's College London and Rutgers University in New Jersey created a modified enzyme (a protein that speeds up chemical reactions) that breaks down polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic 10 times quicker, using 10 times less enzyme. They accomplished this just by changing the liquid it works in and making small changes to the enzyme's structure.

mix_items.title: A personality trait may provide clues to functioning in frontotemporal dementia
mix_items.summary: Frontotemporal dementia often results in early changes in personality or behavior before changes in cognitive skills. People with this condition who have lower levels of conscientiousness, a personality trait related to organization, reliability and planning, may be more likely to have problems with their ability to complete everyday activities, according to a study published in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Financial institutions tout sustainability while still funding high-carbon projects, review finds
mix_items.summary: A review published in the International Journal of Managerial and Financial Accounting on the subject of greenwashing in financial services has found that financial institutions often claim environmental responsibility while continuing to finance high-carbon projects.

mix_items.title: How babies are born knowing the difference between day and night
mix_items.summary: Before a baby sees its first sunrise, it is already receiving signals about day and night. Melatonin, a hormone released mainly at night, can pass from the mother through the placenta. The placenta supplies the developing fetus with oxygen and nutrients.

mix_items.title: Protein-building RNA molecules reveal possible remnants of an ancestral genetic code
mix_items.summary: The genetic code determines the correspondence between genetic instructions and amino acids—the building blocks that form proteins. How this correspondence arose is one of the major open questions in evolutionary biology. A study led by Dr. Lluís Ribas de Pouplana, ICREA researcher at IRB Barcelona, and Dr. Paul Schimmel, with the participation of researchers from MIT and Scripps Research, has identified conserved signals in transfer RNAs that could help reconstruct the early stages of this system.

mix_items.title: New MRI scan 'color codes' treatment-resistant cancer cells, sparing some patients from aggressive treatment
mix_items.summary: Scientists are developing a new MRI-based test that could spare thousands of cancer patients from aggressive radiotherapy treatment.

mix_items.title: Tiny sensor could track blood pressure continuously without inflatable cuff
mix_items.summary: A tiny sensor could one day measure blood pressure continuously, comfortably and accurately without an inflatable cuff. The device was developed by professors Amir Rosenthal and Daniel Lange of the Technion's Andrew and Erna Viterbi Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering, together with doctoral student Gil Gelbert. They published their findings in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Webb's controversial 'little red dots' may finally have an explanation
mix_items.summary: Astronomers may have solved one of the biggest mysteries uncovered by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), using sophisticated simulations to show that enigmatic objects known as "little red dots" (LRDs) are likely the birthplaces of the first supermassive black holes.

mix_items.title: Protein tails help shape mosquito cell-to-cell channels
mix_items.summary: Cells share small molecules with their neighbors through tiny tunnels made of proteins arranged in a ring. Research at Nagoya University suggests that the tails of the proteins must link up to form an inner ring for the tunnel to become evenly round—a previously unknown step in how these cell-to-cell connections are built.

mix_items.title: Two new howler monkey species discovered in the Amazon after 85 years
mix_items.summary: Genetic research has uncovered two previously unknown species of howler monkey living in the Amazon rainforest, confirming the world's largest tropical forest is more biodiverse than scientists thought.

mix_items.title: Predicting long-term pain after freezing nerves in surgery
mix_items.summary: After thoracic surgery—any medical operation done inside the chest—patients can experience pain, soreness or numbness even years later. This is because the incisions cut through muscles and nerves on sensitive ribs, which can cause damage and inflammation.

mix_items.title: When the definition of sexual consent gets stretched
mix_items.summary: Men in treatment for domestic violence have an elastic view of what constitutes consent in their partner, an UdeM study has found.

mix_items.title: Repeatable laser measurements reveal 'forbidden' vibrations in single molecules without destroying them
mix_items.summary: The possibility of controlling "forbidden" excitations of vibrations in molecules could form the basis of extremely accurate clocks, quantum bits and precise tests of the fundamental laws of physics. Researchers at the University of Basel have now identified and controlled such "forbidden" transitions in single isolated nitrogen molecules without destroying them.

mix_items.title: Beat it: Den Staat farmers in South Africa use drumming and fire to deter elephants
mix_items.summary: “Last night we had a very big fight with an elephant in our tomato field,” said Joeman Moyo, a farmer at Den Staat farm in South Africa’s Limpopo region. “We used a torch … to make a fire. The elephant would go away but return when I put out the torch. I also burned a […]

mix_items.title: Is your gym attire setting you up for health problems?
mix_items.summary: Kenya’s fitness boom runs on activewear built for stretch, sweat and shine yet almost no one asks what’s actually in the fabric. By 7 a.m. on a Saturday, Riverside Square in Nairobi’s Westlands neighborhood is already filling up. Dozens arrive in matching leggings and sports bras, water bottles clipped to armbands, ready for a running […]

mix_items.title: Daily, oral GLP-1 medication reduced episodes of sleep apnea in adults with excess weight
mix_items.summary: Adults with moderate-to-severe sleep apnea and excess weight had significantly fewer episodes of breathing interruptions while sleeping after taking the daily oral GLP-1 medication orforglipron for one year, compared with adults in the placebo group, according to new, independent, preliminary late-breaking science presented Monday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago.

mix_items.title: Airborne imaging explores a mosaic of thawing permafrost
mix_items.summary: Permafrost in many of Earth's northern regions is thawing, a process that unlocks greenhouse gases, threatens infrastructure, and could alter landscapes and ecosystems. The Arctic and subarctic are vast, and gaining a comprehensive picture of permafrost distribution is difficult, as it requires seeing under the ground. Now, with a new method that can map permafrost from the air, researchers may get a much more spatially cohesive view of permafrost thickness and distribution.

mix_items.title: What university campus sewage can reveal about the effects of exam stress
mix_items.summary: It is not often that scientists take a keen interest in the sewage produced by students. But a study of wastewater from a university campus in Australia is revealing insights into how exam stress affects the body that traditional surveys may miss.

mix_items.title: Reef biodiversity accounting to help scale up restoration
mix_items.summary: To encourage new investments in more effective reef restoration activities, Australian scientists are recommending a new way of measuring biodiversity on coral reefs. A team of Australian environmental scientists led by James Cook University's distinguished professor Morgan Pratchett proposes the more rigorous and transparent framework in a paper published in the journal One Earth.

mix_items.title: Leader still means man, and language does not change that, according to study
mix_items.summary: Can gender-inclusive language weaken the deeply ingrained stereotype that a political leader is a man? A recent international study, conducted in 42 countries and involving researchers from SWPS University, shows that introducing such forms into language has little impact on how the public perceives political leaders.

mix_items.title: NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities
mix_items.summary: Launched nearly 50 years ago in 1977, NASA’s Voyager 1 on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will have traveled one light-day from Earth, which is more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, and any light from Earth would take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. NASA will highlight […]

mix_items.title: US stakes competing claims to Pacific seabed mining areas, challenging UN authority
mix_items.summary: A recent Mongabay investigation by Elizabeth Claire Alberts and Andrés Alegría reveals that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a swath of deep sea regulated by the International Seabed Authority, has received a surge of claim applications filed with the United States for mineral exploration and exploitation. While the ISA, a U.N.-associated body, is […]

mix_items.title: EEG analysis estimates depressive symptom severity in adults not receiving psychiatric treatment
mix_items.summary: Researchers at University of Tsukuba have developed a method that uses brainwave patterns to estimate the severity of self-reported depressive symptoms in adults who are not receiving treatment. The method examines how abrupt timing shifts in brain rhythms at one recording site are associated with those at another, and could support future screening and symptom monitoring. The work is published in Nature Mental Health.

mix_items.title: Study finds links between bacteria in wastewater and chronic disease
mix_items.summary: Bacteria found in wastewater may provide clues about community health, including rates of chronic disease, health behaviors and social conditions, according to a recent study from The Ohio State University.

mix_items.title: Norovirus No. 1 cause of cruise ship outbreaks for past 30 years, but other pathogens gaining
mix_items.summary: The gastrointestinal (GI) pathogen norovirus was the leading cause of infectious-disease outbreaks on cruise ships over the past 57 years, but respiratory pathogens such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2 also emerged as important contributors, reveals a meta-analysis published in eClinicalMedicine.

mix_items.title: Free-to-air TV failures add to data costs for remote Australian First Nations households
mix_items.summary: Almost two in three respondents surveyed in Australia's remote First Nations communities did not have working free-to-air television, a study has found.

mix_items.title: Q&A: 'AI has become a major force shaping our world,' says expert
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is reshaping research, economies, and everyday life at a remarkable speed. In this interview accompanying the new AI100 report, Iyad Rahwan reflects on the rise of generative AI, the growing concentration of AI power, and the challenges facing societies worldwide. He also explains why Europe must seize this "Sputnik moment" and why he remains optimistic about AI's potential to accelerate scientific discovery.

mix_items.title: Resistance training key to maintaining muscle function during GLP-1 weight loss, study shows
mix_items.summary: A study has revealed that resistance (weight) training not only preserves lean and muscle mass but also increases strength in people taking weight-loss medication. Published in Nature Medicine, the Tirzepatide and Resistance Exercise (T-REx) study is the first to show the effects of combining a GLP-1 medicine and resistance training on body composition, muscle mass, strength and a range of cardiovascular health measures.

mix_items.title: Uncovering the regulators of inflammatory responses in macrophages
mix_items.summary: Macrophages are white blood cells that serve as the first line of defense against infections. When they encounter harmful pathogens or bacteria, macrophages undergo metabolic reprogramming: significant metabolic changes that facilitate the production of inflammatory molecules.

mix_items.title: Archaeological trap: Fish can make skeletons appear hundreds of years too old
mix_items.summary: The Danish town of Svendborg was once home to a Franciscan monastery. As at other monasteries in Denmark, it was considered highly prestigious to be buried as close to the monastery church as possible, preferably inside the church itself, for instance near the chapter house or along the cloister.

mix_items.title: ‘You need strong willpower’: IUCN’s Kazi Zenifar Azmiri on being a woman wildlife biologist
mix_items.summary: For more than a decade, Kazi Zenifar Azmiri has played a crucial part in protecting wildlife in Bangladesh. Zenifar is a program associate at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). Her work centers primarily on the rescue and rehabilitation of threatened vultures like the white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Himalayan griffon vulture (Gyps […]

mix_items.title: Ph.D. completion depends on reciprocal mix of candidate, supervision and institution, review finds
mix_items.summary: Low Ph.D. completion rates remain a challenge in higher education, reflecting a complex interplay of individual, supervisory and institutional factors. Despite extensive research, few reviews have investigated the factors related to Ph.D. completion, with most focusing on isolated aspects, such as supervision or mental health.

mix_items.title: Almost one in four Americans believe misinformation about the cause of autism
mix_items.summary: Nearly a quarter of Americans believe that childhood vaccines and taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) during pregnancy cause autism, despite no evidence to support those claims, a survey published in JAMA Health Forum notes. The findings suggest that misinformation about autism persists and that better public health messaging is needed to combat it.

mix_items.title: Older female influencers challenging stereotypes around aging
mix_items.summary: Older female influencers are using social media to challenge long-held assumptions about women and aging, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

mix_items.title: New stem cell models reveal how earliest human placenta structures take shape
mix_items.summary: The placenta is essential for a healthy pregnancy, but the earliest steps of its formation have been hidden from scientific view. Now Columbia researchers led by Mijo Simunovic have created lab-grown organoids that reconstruct the earliest steps in human placenta formation, offering a powerful new tool for studying how pregnancy begins and why it often fails. The development of the 3D models is described in the current issue of Nature Cell Biology.

mix_items.title: Opioid use can become long-term following surgery
mix_items.summary: Opioids are effective medicines for severe pain following surgery, but prolonged use is associated with risks such as dependence and overdose. In his thesis, Claes Gedda at the Department of Clinical Sciences, Danderyd Hospital, Karolinska Institutet, investigated how common it is for patients in Sweden to continue using opioids after surgery, which patients are at higher risk, and whether usage following major surgery can be reduced.

mix_items.title: Blood pressure meds may improve therapy for ulcerative colitis
mix_items.summary: A class of blood pressure medications may improve a widely used treatment for ulcerative colitis, the most common type of inflammatory bowel disease, suggests a new study, led by Northwestern Medicine and Kiel University in Germany, of thousands of patients with the disease.

mix_items.title: Drought reshapes livelihoods of Kenya’s Daasanach pastoralists, study finds
mix_items.summary: The Daasanach people in the Turkana Basin of northern Kenya experienced the worst drought in 40 years between November 2020 and March 2023. The Daasanach are pastoralists who have lived semi-nomadically for roughly 6,000 years, supported by herds of livestock including cows, camels, donkeys, and goats. A group of researchers worked with the Daasanach to […]

mix_items.title: HIV activism offers a roadmap for tackling weight stigma
mix_items.summary: Although HIV and obesity are not mirror images, lessons from the HIV response could accelerate fairer and more effective care for people living with obesity.

mix_items.title: Axonal defects linked to rare form of Parkinson's disease
mix_items.summary: A genetic mutation linked to Parkinson's disease produced abnormalities in a subset of nerve cells, offering a clue about the disease's causes, according to a new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings offer new clues about how the neurodegenerative disorder begins and progresses, said D. James Surmeier, Ph.D., the Nathan Smith Davis professor and chair of neuroscience, who was a co-author of the study.

mix_items.title: Visual tests could indicate cognitive decline—study
mix_items.summary: Simple visual tests could be an early indicator of cognitive decline, a precursor to dementia, according to a new study published in the journal Brain Sciences.

mix_items.title: Greta Thunberg arrives at UN climate talks saying ‘everything we love is at stake’

mix_items.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
mix_items.summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

mix_items.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
mix_items.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
mix_items.summary: Deep inside a high-altitude Chinese cave, scientists discovered a ghostly, eyeless freshwater snail that has evolved to live entirely in darkness, marking the first recorded discovery of its kind in China. Named after a faceless mythical creature, the rare species may already be in danger, with researchers finding only three living adults.
